practice_questions.text:
Which mechanical property describes the ability of a material to be drawn into a wire without fracturing?
A) Hardness
B) Brittleness
C) Ductility
D) Stiffness
practice_questions.marks: C) Ductility [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'toughness' in the context of engineering materials.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks awarded for each valid point up to 2:
• The ability to absorb energy before fracturing / the ability to deform plastically before breaking
• A tough material gives warning before failure / does not shatter suddenly
• Example: mild steel, nylon [1 mark for the concept, 1 mark for additional detail or named example]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why cast iron is described as brittle and explain why this affects where it can be used in engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per reason up to 2:
• It fractures suddenly with little or no plastic deformation before breaking
• It cannot absorb impact energy; it shatters without visible warning
• Therefore it must not be used where sudden impact loads are expected (e.g. not suitable for vehicle body panels, safety helmets)

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is designing a set of precision cutting tools for a CNC workshop. Explain how the mechanical properties of hardness and toughness both influence the material choice for the cutting tools, and discuss the trade-off between these two properties.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Clear explanation of hardness (resists surface wear and indentation, measured by Brinell or Vickers test) linked specifically to cutting tools (must scratch the workpiece without being worn away). Clear explanation of toughness (absorbs impact energy before fracturing) and why low toughness in a very hard steel creates brittle fracture risk under cutting forces. Explicit discussion of trade-off: increasing hardness through heat treatment reduces toughness; tool steels are therefore tempered after hardening to recover some toughness.
Secure (3-4): Both properties named and linked to cutting tools; trade-off mentioned but explanation of the mechanism may be limited.
Developing (2): One property explained adequately; second mentioned without development.
Emerging (1): A correct property named with no engineering context.

practice_questions.text:
The table below gives information about three materials:
- Material A: brittle, high compressive strength, low tensile strength, good vibration damping
- Material B: ductile, high tensile strength, malleable, moderate hardness
- Material C: very hard, low ductility, resists surface wear

Match each material to one suitable engineering application and give a reason for each choice.
Applications: (i) structural beam in a building frame (ii) machine-tool cutting insert (iii) machine bed to support a lathe
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): All three matched correctly with a relevant property as reason:
• Material B → structural beam: ductile and high tensile strength so it can support suspended loads and gives warning deformation before failure
• Material C → cutting insert: very hard and resists surface wear so it can cut workpiece materials without losing its edge quickly
• Material A → machine bed: brittle and high compressive strength; the lathe bed is under compressive load, and its vibration-damping property absorbs machining vibrations
Secure (3-4): Two correct matches with reasons; third may be incorrect or lack reasoning.
Developing (2): One correct match with a valid reason.
Emerging (1): Material named or application identified without linking to a specific property.

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Engineering Ltd is designing a new safety barrier for a car park. The barrier must flex when struck by a slow-moving vehicle and return to its original position without permanent deformation, while also being hard-wearing on its surface.

Evaluate the importance of mechanical properties in choosing a suitable material for this barrier. In your answer, consider at least three different mechanical properties and justify which is most important for this application.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): At least three properties identified (e.g. toughness/elasticity to absorb impact and spring back; hardness for surface wear resistance; stiffness — not too stiff or it will fracture instead of flexing). Each is clearly linked to the specific requirement (slow vehicle impact, spring-back, hard-wearing surface). A justified conclusion states which property is most critical and why (e.g. toughness / elastic recovery is most important because the barrier's primary function is repeated impact absorption without permanent deformation; hardness is secondary). Response reads as a balanced evaluation, not a list.
Secure (5-6): Three properties identified with reasonable links to the application; conclusion present but may lack full justification.
Developing (3-4): Two properties identified; links to application may be partial; conclusion may be missing.
Emerging (1-2): One or two properties named with minimal engineering reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a system block diagram?
A) A diagram using standard electrical component symbols to show how parts are wired
B) A diagram using labelled rectangles and arrows to show how sub-systems are linked
C) A diagram using ovals and diamonds to show the sequence of steps in a process
D) A photograph of a product showing all its internal components
practice_questions.marks: B) A diagram using labelled rectangles and arrows to show how sub-systems are linked [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between an open-loop control system and a closed-loop control system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct difference, up to 2 marks:
- Open-loop has no feedback path; closed-loop has a feedback path that monitors the output.
- Open-loop output cannot correct itself if conditions change; closed-loop adjusts the process to match the desired output.
- Open-loop is simpler/cheaper to build; closed-loop is more accurate but more complex.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A designer is creating a block diagram for an automatic greenhouse temperature control system. The system uses a temperature sensor, a microcontroller and a fan motor.

Name the correct flowchart symbol for each of the following:
(a) START
(b) “Read temperature sensor”
(c) “Is temperature above 25°C?”
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Oval / terminator [1 mark]
(b) Parallelogram / input-output symbol [1 mark]
(c) Diamond / decision box [1 mark]
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Control Ltd is designing an automated paint-mixing machine. The machine reads a colour code from a barcode, mixes the correct pigments and fills a tin.

Draw and label a system block diagram for this machine. Your diagram should show at least three sub-systems and indicate the direction of signal flow.
practice_questions.type: 5 marks — Complete the Flowchart or System Diagram
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for the following:
- INPUT sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. barcode scanner / colour code input) [1 mark]
- At least one PROCESS sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. microcontroller / mixing controller) [1 mark]
- OUTPUT sub-system correctly labelled (e.g. pigment valves / tin-filling actuator) [1 mark]
- Arrows showing correct direction of signal/material flow between blocks [1 mark]
- Diagram uses rectangles only (no component symbols, no flowchart shapes) [1 mark]
[5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a schematic drawing and a system block diagram. In your answer, state when an engineer would use each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A schematic uses standard component symbols (e.g. resistor zigzag, capacitor lines) to show how components are wired; a block diagram uses labelled rectangles to show how sub-systems are linked.
- A schematic is used when a technician needs to build or fault-find a circuit; a block diagram is used at the planning stage to show the overall system structure before detailed design.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Automation Ltd manufactures industrial ovens used in a food factory. The oven must maintain a temperature of 180°C. A sensor inside the oven measures the actual temperature every 10 seconds and feeds the reading back to a controller, which switches the heating elements on or off as needed.

Evaluate whether a closed-loop or open-loop control system is the better choice for this oven. Use engineering reasoning to justify your answer.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed comparison of open-loop and closed-loop systems applied to the oven context. Explains that open-loop (e.g. a fixed timer) would cause temperature drift if the ambient conditions change, door is opened or batch size varies, resulting in inconsistent food quality or safety hazards. Clearly explains how the closed-loop arrangement described (sensor feeds back to controller, controller switches heating) corrects deviations from 180°C automatically, ensuring consistent output. Considers a disadvantage of closed-loop (more complex, sensor can fail) and reaches a justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Correct identification of the system as closed-loop. Explains the benefit of feedback (auto-correction) and links it to the oven application. Some comparison with open-loop but may not fully develop the disadvantage or link to engineering consequences.

Developing (3-4): Describes the closed-loop system broadly. May correctly identify that feedback improves accuracy without explaining the mechanism. Limited comparison.

Emerging (1-2): Simple statement that closed-loop is better with minimal justification. May confuse open and closed loop.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes fused deposition modelling (FDM)?
A) A laser cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer
B) A laser fuses metal powder layer by layer
C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer
D) A router cuts a 3D shape from a solid block of plastic
practice_questions.marks: C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the file format used to transfer a 3D CAD model to an additive manufacturing machine.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Name a Material or Process
practice_questions.marks: STL (Standard Tessellation Language / stereolithography file) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why an engineer might choose additive manufacturing rather than injection moulding to produce a prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- No tooling (mould) required, so there is no tooling cost for a one-off part
- Design can be changed quickly in CAD and re-printed, allowing rapid iteration
- Can produce complex internal geometries or undercuts that moulding cannot
- Short lead time — a prototype can be ready in hours rather than weeks
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in producing a part using fused deposition modelling (FDM).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four of the following stages in a logical order:
1. Create or obtain a 3D CAD model of the part
2. Export/save the model as an STL file
3. Import the STL file into slicing software; set layer thickness and generate support structures
4. The heated nozzle melts thermoplastic filament and extrudes it onto the build platform
5. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools; the platform lowers by one layer thickness
6. The process repeats until the part is complete; support material is removed
[4 marks — 1 mark per valid stage, must be in a logical manufacturing order]

practice_questions.text:
Holbrook Designs Ltd is a product design studio developing a new ergonomic handle for a power tool. The studio needs three prototypes to present to the client next week. The final product will be injection moulded in ABS in quantities of 50,000 units per year.

Evaluate whether additive manufacturing is a suitable choice for producing the three prototypes. In your answer, consider the advantages and limitations of additive manufacturing for this situation compared with other available methods.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear evaluation of both additive manufacturing and at least one alternative, with advantages and limitations linked explicitly to the details of the scenario (3 prototypes, one-week deadline, eventual high-volume injection moulding). A justified conclusion about whether additive manufacturing is suitable.

Secure (5-6 marks): Advantages and limitations both addressed with some link to the scenario. Some comparison made. Conclusion present but may be underdeveloped.

Developing (3-4 marks): Advantages or limitations covered but not both. Limited link to scenario specifics. Conclusion weak or absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points about 3D printing with little or no reference to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
Advantages for this scenario: no tooling cost for 3 units; STL file can be printed within the one-week deadline; design iteration is possible if changes arise; complex ergonomic geometry (curves, grip features) is achievable.
Limitations: surface finish may show layer lines (may not matter for internal client presentation but matters if the prototype is for a consumer show); material properties of FDM ABS differ from injection-moulded ABS; printing 3 units still takes several hours each.
Alternative: hand-carved foam or machined model — slower and less accurate for ergonomic geometry.
Conclusion: additive manufacturing (FDM or SLA) is well suited for this low-volume rapid prototyping task, but the studio should note that the final product will require injection moulding tooling investment before volume production.

practice_questions.text: Compare stereolithography (SLA) and metal sintering as additive manufacturing processes. In your answer, refer to the materials used, the energy source, the surface finish achieved and a typical application for each.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for developed comparative points. Up to 6 marks across the four areas:

Materials: SLA uses liquid photopolymer resin; metal sintering uses fine metal powder (e.g. stainless steel, titanium, aluminium alloy).

Energy source: SLA uses an ultraviolet laser to cure/harden the resin; metal sintering uses a high-powered infrared laser to fuse the powder particles.

Surface finish: SLA produces a very smooth surface finish with fine detail, better than FDM; metal sintering produces a rough surface with powder particles and may need machining or polishing where a smooth finish is required.

Typical application: SLA — appearance prototypes, dental models, jewellery; metal sintering — aerospace turbine components, medical implants, lightweight structural brackets.

[6 marks — must compare, not just describe each in isolation. 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks for a developed comparative point. Max 6.]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes reciprocating motion?
A) Spinning continuously around a fixed axis
B) Moving in a straight line in one direction only
C) Moving back and forth along a straight line
D) Swinging around a fixed point
practice_questions.marks: C) Moving back and forth along a straight line [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Name the type of motion produced by each of the following:
(a) A motor shaft spinning
(b) A piston moving inside a cylinder
(c) A windscreen wiper arm
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Rotary motion [1 mark]
(b) Reciprocating motion [1 mark]
(c) Oscillating motion [1 mark]
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the shape of a cam profile controls the movement of a follower.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- The follower's position depends on the radius of the cam at the point of contact.
- Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up; where the radius is small, the follower drops down.
- The profile (outline shape) of the cam is designed to create the desired movement pattern in the follower.
[2 marks — both marks require a link between cam profile/radius and follower position]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a crank and slider mechanism converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion. Your answer should refer to the key components involved.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 4 marks:
- A crank (offset pin or arm) is attached to a rotating shaft.
- A connecting rod links the crank pin to a slider (piston or sliding block).
- As the crank rotates, the connecting rod pushes and pulls the slider.
- The slider moves back and forth in a straight line (reciprocating motion).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Westbrook Machinery Ltd manufactures food-packaging equipment. One machine uses a cam mechanism to open and close a packaging flap 60 times per minute. The flap must open slowly and close quickly to allow product to fall in without jamming.

Which cam profile would be most suitable for this application? Explain your choice.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Correctly identifies the pear cam profile and gives a detailed explanation linking the profile shape to the required motion: the long, gradually curving lobe allows slow opening of the flap, while the short, sharp drop on the pear’s ‘nose’ produces the quick closing action. Explains the mechanism by which the follower position is set by the cam radius, and links this to the packaging application (product falls through without jamming).

Secure (3-4): Correctly identifies pear cam. Explains that it produces a slow rise and a quick drop, linked to the requirement. May not fully explain the cam-radius mechanism.

Developing (2): Names a plausible cam type with a partial explanation.

Emerging (1): Names a cam profile with no explanation.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Galton Engineering produces bicycle brake assemblies. The brake lever is connected to the brake pads by a cable and a bell-crank linkage.

Evaluate whether using a bell-crank (reverse) linkage is the best mechanism for this application. In your answer, consider at least one alternative mechanism and compare them.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains that a bell-crank linkage changes the direction of motion by 90°, allowing the cable tension from the hand lever (pulling along the handlebar) to be redirected to push brake pads perpendicular to the cable. Evaluates advantages (compact, reliable, no power loss, easily adjusted) and limitations (friction at pivot, requires correct alignment, cable stretch over time). Considers an alternative (direct pull cable, hydraulic disc brake) and compares it on relevant grounds (force, weight, cost, maintenance). Reaches a justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Explains the function of the bell-crank in changing motion direction, at least one advantage and one limitation, and some comparison with an alternative.

Developing (3-4): Partial explanation of the linkage function. Limited comparison with alternatives.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of a linkage with minimal engineering reasoning.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following metals is classified as ferrous?
A) Aluminium
B) Copper
C) Low carbon steel
D) Zinc
practice_questions.marks: C) Low carbon steel [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between low carbon steel and high carbon steel.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid difference up to 2:
• Low carbon steel has lower carbon content (0.1–0.3%) than high carbon steel (0.6–1.4%)
• Low carbon steel is more ductile and easier to weld; high carbon steel is harder and more brittle
• High carbon steel can be hardened by quenching; low carbon steel does not respond to this treatment

practice_questions.text: Name one metal alloy and identify the two main elements it is made from.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Name a Material or Process
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks awarded for a correct alloy with its constituent elements:
• Brass: copper and zinc
• Bronze: copper and tin
• Stainless steel: iron, carbon and chromium (accept iron + chromium)
[1 mark for a correctly paired alloy and elements]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of hardening high carbon steel by quenching. Your answer should include what happens to the steel's crystal structure during the process.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct stage/point up to 4:
• Heat the steel above its critical temperature (approximately 723°C or above)
• Hold at temperature to allow the structure to become austenite throughout
• Rapidly cool by plunging into water or oil (quenching)
• Rapid cooling traps a hard, brittle crystal structure called martensite / prevents the slower transformation back to softer ferrite and pearlite
[4 marks — each stage must be in logical order for full marks]

practice_questions.text:
Marrowbone Engineering Ltd makes a corner bracket from low carbon steel by bending sheet material. A quality inspector asks the engineer why high carbon steel was not chosen for the same bracket.

Explain why low carbon steel is a more suitable choice than high carbon steel for a bent sheet-metal bracket, referring to at least two relevant mechanical properties.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two or more properties identified and clearly linked to the manufacturing process and application. For example: ductility — low carbon steel can be plastically deformed by bending without fracturing at the bend radius, whereas high carbon steel would crack; malleability — it can be pressed and formed without breaking; weldability — low carbon steel can be welded to adjacent components without risk of heat-affected-zone cracking. Discussion of why high carbon steel would be unsuitable (less ductile, brittle at bend radius, more difficult to weld).
Secure (3-4): Two properties identified with valid links; explanation of why high carbon steel fails may be limited.
Developing (2): One property identified and linked to the application adequately.
Emerging (1): A correct property named with no development.

practice_questions.text:
Crane & Hatch, a Birmingham fabrication workshop, needs to select a metal for two different components: (a) a precision gear that must resist surface wear from meshing contact, and (b) an electrical bus bar that must conduct electricity efficiently along its full length.

Evaluate the suitability of high carbon steel and copper for each component, explaining how the properties of each metal match or conflict with the requirements of each application.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Considers all four combinations (high carbon steel for gear, high carbon steel for bus bar, copper for gear, copper for bus bar). High carbon steel: high hardness after quenching — excellent for gear (resists wear from mesh contact); poor conductor — unsuitable for bus bar. Copper: excellent electrical and thermal conductor — ideal for bus bar; low hardness and ductile — will wear quickly at gear mesh contact, so unsuitable. Conclusion identifies that neither metal performs well in both roles — each must be matched to the application it suits. Response is structured as an evaluation, not a list.
Secure (5-6): Both metals evaluated against at least two requirements; conclusion present but may not consider all four combinations.
Developing (3-4): Each metal given one relevant property; limited cross-comparison.
Emerging (1-2): One metal addressed or properties listed without application links.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes non-destructive testing?
A) Testing that always requires the component to be broken to measure fracture energy
B) Testing that checks the component without damaging it, so it can still be used
C) Testing that uses hardness indentation to measure surface resistance
D) Testing that can only be carried out on plastic components
practice_questions.marks: B) Testing that checks the component without damaging it, so it can still be used [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one destructive test and one non-destructive test used in engineering. For each, describe how it is carried out.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Destructive test — any one of (tensile test / Vickers hardness / Rockwell hardness / Brinell hardness / Charpy impact test):
Accept a description including: the specimen is prepared, force/load is applied, outcome is measured numerically (force at fracture / hardness number / energy absorbed), the component is destroyed in the process [2 marks — 1 for naming, 1 for description].

Non-destructive test — any one of (visual inspection / dye penetrant / ultrasonic / radiographic / magnetic particle inspection):
Accept a description including: the method used to detect the defect, the component remains usable afterwards [2 marks — 1 for naming, 1 for description].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between quality assurance and quality control in a manufacturing company.
practice_questions.marks:
Quality assurance: a proactive system of procedures, training and supplier management designed to PREVENT defects from occurring during production [1 mark].
Quality control: reactive inspection and testing of components during or after production to IDENTIFY and reject defective items [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Calderwood Precision Components Ltd machines steel shafts to a nominal diameter of 18.00 mm with a tolerance of ±0.05 mm.
(a) State the upper and lower limits of the acceptable diameter.
(b) A micrometer reading gives a shaft diameter of 17.94 mm. State whether this shaft should be accepted or rejected, and give a reason.
(c) Explain why a GO/NO-GO gauge is preferred over a micrometer for checking these shafts on a high-volume production line.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
(a)
Upper limit: 18.05 mm; Lower limit: 17.95 mm [1 mark]

(b)
17.94 mm is below the lower limit of 17.95 mm, so the shaft is REJECTED [1 mark].

(c)
Mastering: GO/NO-GO gauge provides a fast pass/fail decision without reading a numerical value; on a high-volume line where hundreds of shafts are checked per hour, the speed advantage is critical; the gauge eliminates human reading error associated with interpreting a micrometer scale; trained operatives can use a GO/NO-GO gauge with minimal instruction, reducing labour cost [3 marks from the above points, 1 each, any 3 well-developed points].
Secure: Two well-explained points about speed/simplicity.
Developing: One reason given without full explanation.
Emerging: Vague response — 'easier to use'.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why ultrasonic testing is used to inspect welds in a steel pressure vessel rather than visual inspection.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following:
• Ultrasonic testing detects INTERNAL defects (voids, inclusions, cracks) that visual inspection cannot see on the surface [1 mark].
• The component does not need to be cut open — it remains intact and usable after UT [1 mark].
• UT can inspect through the full thickness of the wall, whereas visual inspection is limited to the surface layer [1 mark].
• UT is more sensitive to crack depth and orientation than visual inspection [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Vanthorpe Aerospace manufactures aluminium wing panels for light aircraft. The panels are high-value components that must be inspected for surface cracks after machining.
(a) Name a suitable NDT method for detecting surface cracks in the aluminium panels.
(b) Describe how this method is carried out.
(c) Explain why destructive testing would not be suitable for this application.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names dye penetrant testing (or equivalent appropriate NDT method). Detailed description of the process (dye applied → capillary action draws dye into cracks → developer applied → dye bleeds back out and is visible). Clear explanation that destructive testing would destroy high-value panels so none would be available for use, and that DT only tests samples whereas NDT can test every component. Answer is logically structured with consistent links between method choice and application.

Secure (5-6): Correct method named and described in 3+ steps. Explanation of why DT is unsuitable is present but may lack full development.

Developing (3-4): Method named correctly; description partial; explanation of DT unsuitability limited.

Emerging (1-2): Method named but no useful description or explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes pressure die casting?
A) Molten metal is poured by gravity into a disposable sand mould
B) Molten metal is injected under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die
C) Sheet metal is squeezed between a punch and die in the solid state
D) Polymer granules are melted and injected into a water-cooled mould
practice_questions.marks: B) Molten metal is injected under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the channel through which molten metal is poured into a sand mould, and name the reservoir that compensates for metal shrinkage during cooling.
practice_questions.marks:
Sprue (vertical pouring channel) [1 mark].
Riser / feeder (reservoir that compensates for shrinkage) [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages of producing an aluminium component using sand casting.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four stages in a logical order:
- Place the pattern in the drag; ram sand around it
- Add cope, form sprue and riser channels; separate halves and remove pattern
- Place any cores required for internal voids; reassemble and secure mould
- Pour molten aluminium through the sprue until metal rises at the riser
- Allow to cool and solidify; break away the sand mould
- Remove casting; cut off sprues and risers; fettle and machine to final dimensions
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a draft angle is needed on the pattern used in sand casting and on the walls of an injection mould.
practice_questions.marks:
Sand casting: a draft angle on the pattern walls allows the pattern to be withdrawn cleanly from the compacted sand without collapsing the cavity walls [1 mark].
Injection moulding: a draft angle on the mould wall allows the solidified plastic part to be ejected (pushed out by ejector pins) without jamming or tearing [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Enclosures Ltd manufactures aluminium housings for outdoor electrical distribution boxes. The current production volume is 200 units per year, but a new contract would increase this to 15,000 units per year. The company currently uses sand casting.

Evaluate whether the company should switch to pressure die casting for the higher volume. In your answer, consider tooling cost, surface finish, dimensional accuracy, production rate and any limitations.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced evaluation of both processes with clear links to the scenario details (200 vs 15,000 units/year; aluminium; outdoor electrical housing). Both advantages and limitations addressed for each process. A justified conclusion with reasoning about when the switch becomes economical.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both processes described with some comparison. Most key factors covered. Conclusion present but reasoning may be limited.

Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly descriptive. One process favoured without clear comparison. Scenario details used minimally.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points about casting with little or no link to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
Sand casting: low tooling cost (just the pattern), suitable for low volumes, but slower per part, rough surface finish, less dimensional accuracy, mould destroyed each cycle.
Pressure die casting: high tooling cost (steel die, tens of thousands of pounds), but at 15,000 units/year the cost per part is much lower; faster cycle time (seconds); better surface finish and tighter tolerances suitable for precision enclosures; die lasts tens of thousands of cycles.
Limitation of die casting: suitable for aluminium (non-ferrous) so material is compatible; but design changes require expensive die modification.
Conclusion: at 200 units/year sand casting is appropriate; at 15,000 units/year the die cost is easily amortised and die casting is the better choice for speed, accuracy and consistency.

practice_questions.text: Compare injection moulding and press forming as processes for manufacturing a 1 mm thick flat cover panel. In your answer, consider the material used, the tooling required, the production rate and the type of industries that use each process.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Material: injection moulding uses thermoplastics (e.g. ABS, polypropylene); press forming uses sheet metal (steel, aluminium).
Tooling: both require an expensive metal tool (injection mould; punch and die set) suitable for high-volume production.
Production rate: both are fast once tooling is set up — injection moulding cycles in 15-60 seconds; press forming can stamp thousands of panels per hour on high-speed presses.
Industries: injection moulding dominates consumer electronics, packaging and automotive interior trim; press forming dominates automotive body panels, white-goods casings and structural metalwork.
Key difference: injection moulding cannot produce metal panels; press forming cannot produce polymer parts. Material dictates the process.
[6 marks — 1 mark per valid point; 2 marks for a developed comparative point. Marks awarded for comparison, not description in isolation.]

practice_questions.text: A gear train has a driver gear with 24 teeth and a driven gear with 96 teeth. Calculate the gear ratio.
practice_questions.marks:
Gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth [1 mark for correct formula]
= 96 ÷ 24 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= 4:1 [1 mark for correct answer with ratio notation]
[3 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error]
Note: accept 4 or 4.0 without ratio notation for 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
A workshop hoist uses a block-and-tackle with 5 rope sections to lift a heavy machine component weighing 1500 N.

(a) State the velocity ratio of the pulley system.
(b) Calculate the effort force required, assuming ideal (frictionless) conditions.
(c) Explain why the actual effort needed would be higher than your calculated value.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Velocity ratio = 5 [1 mark]
(b) In ideal conditions MA = VR = 5
Effort = load ÷ MA = 1500 ÷ 5 = 300 N [1 mark for method, 1 mark for correct answer with unit]
(c) In a real system, friction in the pulleys and rope wastes energy, so more input force (effort) is required to move the same load / real MA is less than VR. [1 mark]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Give two distinct reasons why a pulley system is used in a vehicle engine workshop to lift an engine out of a car.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct reason, up to 2 marks:
- It reduces the force (effort) needed to lift the heavy engine by multiplying the input force.
- It changes the direction of effort — the technician pulls down on the rope while the load moves upward.
- It allows a single person to lift a load that would otherwise require multiple people.
- It provides a controlled lift, reducing the risk of sudden movement.
[2 marks — must name the mechanism/benefit, not just 'easier' or 'quicker' alone]

practice_questions.text:
Norcroft Robotics Ltd designs a robotic arm. The arm joint is driven by an electric motor with a pinion gear of 15 teeth meshing with a large gear of 90 teeth. The large gear then meshes with a second pinion of 10 teeth, which drives a final output gear of 50 teeth.

Calculate the overall gear ratio of this compound gear train.
practice_questions.marks:
Stage 1 ratio = driven ÷ driver = 90 ÷ 15 = 6 [1 mark]
Stage 2 ratio = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 [1 mark]
Overall ratio = 6 × 5 = 30:1 [1 mark for method (multiply stages), 1 mark for correct answer]
[4 marks — method marks awarded for each stage even if overall answer wrong]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a ball bearing is used instead of a plain bearing in a high-speed electric motor shaft. Your answer should refer to the function of a ball bearing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A ball bearing uses rolling contact (steel balls in a hardened race) rather than sliding contact.
- Rolling contact significantly reduces friction between the rotating shaft and the housing.
- Less friction means lower energy losses as heat, longer component life, and the shaft can rotate at higher speeds without overheating.
[2 marks — answers that only say 'allows rotation' or 'spins' without mentioning friction reduction score zero]

practice_questions.text:
Harwick Elevators Ltd is designing a goods hoist for a warehouse. The engineers must choose between a chain-and-sprocket drive and a belt-and-pulley drive to transmit power from the motor to the lifting drum.

Evaluate which drive system is the better choice for this application. In your answer, consider the advantages and disadvantages of each system.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed comparison of chain-and-sprocket vs belt-and-pulley. Chain: no slip (positive engagement with teeth), high load capacity, suitable for heavy goods hoist, needs lubrication, noisy, more expensive. Belt: quieter, cheaper, some slip possible under high load (safety benefit in a jam but reliability concern for a hoist), no lubrication needed, can accommodate slight misalignment. Evaluates each property against the warehouse goods hoist context (heavy loads, frequent use, reliability critical). Reaches a justified conclusion with engineering reasoning.

Secure (5-6): Identifies key differences (slip vs no-slip, lubrication, cost) and links at least two to the hoist context. Some evaluation but may not cover all relevant factors.

Developing (3-4): Describes one system more fully than the other. Limited comparison. May list properties without linking to the application.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of one drive system with minimal comparison.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
A) ABS
B) Acrylic
C) Polycarbonate
D) Epoxy resin
practice_questions.marks: D) Epoxy resin [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid difference up to 2:
• Thermoplastics soften when reheated and can be reshaped; thermosets cannot be softened by reheating once cured
• Thermosets form permanent cross-links between molecular chains during curing; thermoplastics do not form permanent cross-links
• Thermoplastics are generally recyclable; thermosets are not
• Thermosets generally have better heat and chemical resistance than thermoplastics

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why carbon-fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is used for the fuselage of modern commercial aircraft rather than aluminium alloy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per reason up to 2:
• CFRP has a higher stiffness-to-weight ratio / lower density for equivalent stiffness compared to aluminium alloy
• CFRP does not corrode, reducing maintenance requirements compared to aluminium
• CFRP can be shaped into complex aerodynamic profiles in a single moulding, reducing the number of joints
• Higher fatigue resistance, allowing longer service intervals

practice_questions.text: Explain how the properties of plywood are improved compared to plain structural timber. In your answer, refer to the manufacturing process and the directional properties of wood.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Clear explanation that timber is strong along the grain but weak across it, and that plywood overcomes this by alternating the grain direction of successive veneer layers. This means loads applied in any direction in the plane of the panel are resisted by at least some fibres running along the load direction. Additional points: resists splitting at edges (no single through-grain path); dimensionally stable (opposing grain directions prevent warping); suitable for structural use in both directions (floor decking, concrete formwork). Reference to glue bonding the veneer stack under heat and pressure.
Secure (3-4): Grain-direction principle stated; application linked to at least one advantage.
Developing (2): Identifies that grain is alternated but cannot explain why this improves properties.
Emerging (1): Recognises plywood as an engineered timber product without further explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Fenwick Manufacturing Ltd is designing a protective casing for an outdoor electrical junction box. The casing must be lightweight, electrically insulating, resistant to UV sunlight and able to withstand moderate impact from falling tools.

Evaluate whether polycarbonate or glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) is the more suitable material for this casing.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Both materials evaluated against all four requirements (lightweight, electrical insulation, UV resistance, impact resistance). Polycarbonate: good impact resistance (thermoplastic, deforms before fracturing), electrically insulating, transparent/translucent, however poorer UV resistance without additives — yellows and embrittles over time outdoors. GRP: good UV resistance, electrically insulating, lightweight relative to metals, resists moderate impact; moulded shape is permanent (thermoset matrix); consistent outdoor performance. Justified conclusion identifies GRP as more suitable for long-term outdoor UV exposure, or polycarbonate if transparency/inspection through the casing is also a requirement. Response is balanced and addresses the trade-offs.
Secure (5-6): Both materials covered with valid points against at least two requirements; conclusion present.
Developing (3-4): One material evaluated in detail, second mentioned briefly.
Emerging (1-2): Properties listed without linking to the specific application requirements.

practice_questions.text:
Daleside Pumps is manufacturing a set of conveyor belt seals that must be elastic, tough and resistant to wear from contact with abrasive particles in a slurry stream.

Name the most suitable polymer for these seals and explain why its molecular structure makes it suitable for this application.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Identifies vulcanised rubber. Clear explanation that vulcanisation adds sulfur cross-links between the natural rubber polymer chains. Cross-links allow the rubber to stretch and recover (elasticity), prevent the chains from permanently sliding past each other under load (toughness), and contribute to wear resistance. The cross-linked structure also makes it a thermoset, so it does not soften in the warm slurry environment. All three application requirements (elastic, tough, wear-resistant) are addressed.
Secure (3-4): Vulcanised rubber identified; cross-links mentioned; one or two application links made.
Developing (2): Correct material named; molecular explanation limited or absent.
Emerging (1): Polymer named without reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following line types is used to show a hidden edge on an engineering drawing?
A) A continuous thick line
B) A chain-dotted line
C) A dashed thin line
D) A continuous thin line
practice_questions.marks: C) A dashed thin line [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of information that must be included in the title block of an engineering drawing.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following [1 mark each]:
• Part name / component name
• Drawing number
• Material specification
• Scale
• Projection angle symbol (third-angle)
• Drawn by / date
• General tolerance (e.g. ±0.5 mm unless stated)

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between 2D CAD and 3D CAD (solid modelling). In your answer, give one advantage of 3D CAD over 2D CAD.
practice_questions.marks:
2D CAD produces flat orthographic drawings equivalent to manual drafting [1 mark].
3D CAD creates a virtual solid model from which all 2D views are generated automatically; one advantage — e.g. automatic view generation saves time; designs can be exported directly to CAM with no re-entry; stress analysis (FEA) can be run on the model; client renders and animations can be produced [1 mark — any one valid advantage].

practice_questions.text:
Brightwell Aerospace Ltd is considering switching from manual CNC programming to a fully integrated CAD/CAM workflow for manufacturing aluminium brackets.
(a) Describe what is meant by CAM (computer-aided manufacture).
(b) Give two advantages of a CAD/CAM workflow compared to manual programming for this application.
(c) Identify one potential disadvantage to the company of introducing this new technology.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
(a)
CAM software uses CAD geometry and chosen manufacturing settings to create toolpaths, then post-processes them into machine instructions (G-code) for CNC machines [2 marks — 1 for reference to CAD geometry, 1 for machine instructions].

(b)
Any two of the following [1 mark each, 2 marks total]:
• Faster — toolpaths are generated automatically from CAD geometry, reducing programming time.
• More accurate — removes human errors introduced during manual G-code programming.
• Consistent — the same CAD file produces identical toolpaths every run, supporting repeatable tolerances.
• Integrated — design changes in CAD automatically update the CAM toolpaths, reducing revision time.

(c)
Any one of the following [1 mark]:
• High initial investment in software licences and staff training.
• Staff may need significant upskilling/retraining — existing manual programmers may struggle with the new system.
• Over-reliance on CAD/CAM means a software fault or file error can halt the entire production run.

practice_questions.text: Name and describe one rapid prototyping method used in engineering. Give one advantage of this method compared to producing a prototype by CNC machining.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Method: 3D printing / additive manufacturing (FDM, SLA, SLS — accept any) [1 mark].
Description: a 3D CAD model is sliced into horizontal layers; the machine deposits or cures material layer by layer until the full component is built up [2 marks — 1 for 'layer by layer', 1 for link to 3D CAD input].
Advantage over CNC machining: e.g. no specialist tooling or fixtures required; can produce complex internal geometries that cannot be machined; very fast from digital file to physical part; reduced material waste compared to subtractive machining [1 mark — any one valid point with explanation].

practice_questions.text:
The introduction of robotic automation in a large engineering factory has significant impacts on people and the environment.
Discuss the social and environmental impacts of introducing robotic automation in an engineering factory. In your answer, consider both positive and negative impacts.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Discuss Impact on Society and Environment
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Response covers at least two distinct social impacts (e.g. job displacement for routine operatives balanced against creation of higher-skilled technician/programming roles; improved worker safety by removing humans from hazardous processes) and at least two distinct environmental impacts (e.g. robots can optimise cutting paths to reduce material waste; 24/7 operation increases overall energy consumption). Both positive and negative impacts are balanced for each dimension. Specific mechanisms are stated (not vague generalities). Answer reaches a justified conclusion about the net impact.

Secure (5-6): Social and environmental impacts both addressed, with mostly developed points. Positive and negative balance present but may not be fully justified in the conclusion.

Developing (3-4): Some valid impacts named but many are undeveloped ('robots take jobs', 'better for the environment'). Only one or two dimensions covered.

Emerging (1-2): Generic statements without specific links to automation or the factory context.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'economies of scale' in material purchasing?
A) Buying cheaper materials to reduce quality
B) The reduction in unit cost when ordering larger quantities
C) Using more efficient machines to cut waste
D) Choosing a material with a lower density
practice_questions.marks: B) The reduction in unit cost when ordering larger quantities [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two standard stock forms in which mild steel can be supplied.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Name a Material or Process
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks awarded for any two correct stock forms:
• Sheet / plate
• Bar (square, rectangular or round)
• Tube (circular or square section)
• Angle section / L-section
• Channel section
• Rod / wire
[1 mark for two correct stock forms]

practice_questions.text:
A metal supplier sells 3 mm aluminium sheet in 2000 mm × 1000 mm panels at £48 per panel.
A component is 250 mm × 150 mm. Calculate:
(a) How many components can be cut from one panel.
(b) The material cost per component.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
Step 1 — Five rows of unrotated components: 2000 ÷ 250 = 8 components per row; 5 × 150 = 750 mm of panel width
Step 2 — In the remaining 250 mm width, rotate the components: 2000 ÷ 150 = 13 components
Step 3 — Total per panel: (5 × 8) + 13 = 53 components [2 marks — 1 for correct rounding-down method, 1 for correct total]
Step 4 — Cost per component: £48 ÷ 53 = £0.91 per component [2 marks — 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit]
[Total 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the unit material cost for a prototype component is usually higher than the unit cost for the same component manufactured in a production run of 10,000.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per reason up to 2:
• Fixed costs (delivery, handling, order processing) are spread over fewer units in a prototype batch, raising cost per unit
• Prototype quantities are too small to qualify for bulk-purchase price breaks from the supplier
• The prototype may require material in a non-standard size or specification, increasing cost
• Setup costs for cutting or forming cannot be amortised over enough parts

practice_questions.text:
Aethon Robotics is designing a new agricultural robot chassis. The lead engineer has narrowed the material choice to structural-grade timber (C24) and mild steel box section.

Compare the costs and material properties of these two options, and justify which material you would recommend for a chassis that must support 80 kg of payload and be manufactured in batches of 50 units per month.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Both materials compared on at least three dimensions (cost, strength, weight, availability, machinability/jointing). Timber: lower cost per metre, renewable, easy to cut and drill without specialist equipment, but weaker under dynamic/impact loads, less dimensionally stable in moisture, harder to make neat mechanical joints. Mild steel: higher cost per unit length, heavier, but far superior strength and stiffness per cross-section, dimensionally consistent, weldable, supports repeatable jig-based manufacture at 50/month. At 80 kg payload on an agricultural robot subject to field vibration, mild steel is the stronger recommendation — explicitly justified by dynamic load and dimensional repeatability requirements.
Secure (3-4): Both materials discussed with valid cost and property points; recommendation present but justification may lack specificity.
Developing (2): One material discussed adequately.
Emerging (1): A material named without reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Marrowbone Engineering Ltd uses 4 mm mild steel sheet (1500 mm × 750 mm, £32 per sheet) to produce rectangular brackets measuring 120 mm × 90 mm. Their monthly order is 500 brackets.

Calculate: (a) The number of brackets per sheet. (b) The number of sheets needed per month. (c) The monthly material cost for brackets only. Show all working.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Calculation: Multi-Step with Unit Conversion
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Along 1500 mm: 1500 ÷ 120 = 12 (round down)
Along 750 mm: 750 ÷ 90 = 8 (round down; 750 ÷ 90 = 8.33 → 8)
Brackets per sheet: 12 × 8 = 96 [1 mark]
(b) Sheets per month: 500 ÷ 96 = 5.208… → must round UP to 6 sheets (need whole sheets to get at least 500 brackets) [1 mark]
(c) Monthly cost: 6 × £32 = £192 [1 mark for correct method; 1 mark for correct answer with £ unit]
[Total 4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the brazing process?
A) A filler rod is melted by direct flame contact to form the joint
B) A brass filler rod melts into the joint at around 870 °C while the parent metal remains solid
C) The parent metal is melted and fused together without a filler material
D) A low-melting-point tin alloy is applied below 450 °C to join PCB components
practice_questions.marks: B) A brass filler rod melts into the joint at around 870 °C while the parent metal remains solid [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between brazing and welding.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- Brazing uses a filler rod (brass); welding melts the parent metal itself (may or may not add filler wire)
- Brazing temperature (~870 °C) is below the parent metal melting point; welding exceeds the parent metal melting point (>1500 °C for steel)
- Brazing leaves the parent metal solid; welding fuses the parent metal into a molten pool
- Brazing is typically used for thinner or dissimilar sections; welding produces a higher-strength structural bond
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in riveting two steel plates together. Your answer must include all stages in the correct order.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four stages in correct order. Marking out must be included:
1. Mark out rivet positions using a scriber and rule [must be present]
2. Centre-punch each marked position
3. Clamp the plates together in position
4. Drill rivet holes through both plates with a twist drill
5. De-burr the holes to remove sharp edges
6. Insert rivets through the aligned holes
7. Form/peen the tail into a second head using a rivet snap or rivet gun
[4 marks — deduct a mark if marking out is absent, as stated in examiner guidance]

practice_questions.text:
Complete the sentences below using the correct words from the list.

Brazing / Welding / Soft soldering / Threaded fastening / Riveting

(a) _____ is the only thermal joining process in which the parent metal melts.
(b) _____ uses a brass filler rod at approximately 870 °C without melting the parent metal.
(c) A bolt and nut is an example of a _____, which allows the joint to be disassembled.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Welding [1 mark]
(b) Brazing [1 mark]
(c) Threaded fastening [1 mark]
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Thornfield Fabrications Ltd is producing a mild steel frame for an industrial machine guard. The joints must be strong and permanent. The production supervisor is deciding between MIG welding and brazing.

Evaluate which joining method is more suitable for this application. In your answer consider: joint strength, material compatibility, temperature, production speed and operator skill required.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear evaluation of both methods against the specific scenario (mild steel frame, strong permanent joint, industrial machine guard). Advantages and limitations of each addressed. Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both methods covered with some comparison. Most factors addressed. Conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): One method described in detail; comparison limited. Scenario details used minimally.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points with little reference to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
MIG welding: melts the mild steel parent metal to form a full-penetration fusion bond — very strong, suitable for a structural machine guard frame. Fast deposition rate; suitable for thick steel sections; requires shielding gas supply and operator trained to AWS/CSWIP standard. HAZ (heat-affected zone) may distort thin sections.
Brazing: brass filler at ~870 °C, parent metal does not melt — joint is weaker than a MIG weld for structural steel; not ideal for a heavy machine guard frame under dynamic load. Advantages: less distortion, no shielding gas, smaller heat input.
Conclusion: MIG welding is the better choice for a structural mild steel machine guard frame requiring a strong, permanent joint. Brazing would be suitable for lighter, non-structural assemblies such as pipe fittings or bicycle frames.

practice_questions.text: Give two advantages of using threaded fastenings (bolts and nuts) rather than welding to join the access panels on an industrial machine.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- Panels can be removed for maintenance or inspection without damaging the frame
- No specialist equipment (welder, shielding gas) is needed for assembly or disassembly
- Damaged panels can be individually replaced rather than cutting welds
- Assembly can take place on-site without a welder
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes alternating current (AC)?
A) Current that flows continuously in one direction only
B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave
C) Current produced only by batteries
D) Current that is always at a fixed low voltage
practice_questions.marks: B) Current that reverses direction many times per second, producing a sine wave [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A step-down transformer has 3000 turns on the primary coil and is connected to a 230 V AC supply. The secondary coil has 150 turns.

Calculate the output voltage of the secondary coil.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns [1 mark]
Rearranged: Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 150/3000 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= 11.5 V [1 mark for correct answer with unit]
[3 marks — method marks awarded even if arithmetic error]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using a battery power supply instead of a mains power supply in a portable engineering diagnostic tool.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct advantage, up to 2 marks:
- Batteries are portable — the tool can be used anywhere without needing a mains socket.
- Batteries produce DC directly, which electronic circuits require without additional conversion.
- Battery voltage is low (typically 3–12 V), making the device safer to handle than mains equipment.
- No mains cable required — the technician can move freely around a vehicle or machine.
[2 marks — vague answers like 'cheaper' or 'quicker' without context do not earn marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the function of a relay in an engineered system. Include in your answer:
(a) What the relay does
(b) Why electrical isolation between the two circuits is important
practice_questions.marks:
(a) A relay uses a small control current in an electromagnet/coil to attract an armature/switch contacts, which switches a separate circuit carrying a much larger current. [2 marks — 1 for 'small current controls large current', 1 for electromagnetic/physical mechanism]
(b) Isolation means the high-voltage/high-current power circuit (e.g. 230 V motor) is not electrically connected to the control circuit (e.g. 5 V microcontroller). This prevents high voltage damaging or destroying the sensitive control electronics. [2 marks — 1 for identifying the circuits as separate/not connected, 1 for consequence: protection of electronics]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a motor and a solenoid as output devices in an engineering system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- A motor converts electrical energy into continuous rotary motion; a solenoid converts electrical energy into a single linear push or pull motion.
- Motors are used where sustained rotation is needed (e.g. pump, conveyor); solenoids are used where a short, controlled linear stroke is needed (e.g. door lock, valve).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Elwick Automation Ltd designs a control system for an automated chemical-dosing pump. The pump motor runs on 230 V AC mains. The control circuit uses a microcontroller operating at 5 V DC.

Evaluate the use of a relay to interface the microcontroller with the pump motor. In your answer, consider at least one alternative approach.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Detailed explanation of the relay's function (small 5 V control signal drives coil, which switches the 230 V motor circuit). Evaluates advantages: electrical isolation protects the microcontroller from mains voltage, simple to implement, reliable, easily replaced. Evaluates disadvantages: relay switching is relatively slow (~10 ms), has moving parts that wear, produces a clicking noise. Considers an alternative (solid-state relay or TRIAC/thyristor): no moving parts, faster switching, silent, but more expensive and can fail silently without cutting power (safety concern in a chemical dosing context). Reaches a justified conclusion referencing the application.

Secure (5-6): Explains the isolation benefit clearly. Identifies at least one disadvantage and one alternative with some comparison. Conclusion present but may lack full engineering reasoning.

Developing (3-4): Describes relay function and one advantage. Limited alternative discussion.

Emerging (1-2): Basic relay description with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following energy sources produces radioactive waste rather than greenhouse gases?
A) Coal
B) Natural gas
C) Nuclear
D) Biomass
practice_questions.marks: C) Nuclear [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'planned obsolescence' and give one example of how it is achieved in a consumer product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid point up to 2:
• Planned obsolescence: the deliberate design of a product to become obsolete or fail after a set period, encouraging the customer to purchase a replacement [1 mark]
• Example: sealed non-replaceable batteries in a smartphone or earphone; non-repairable glued construction; styling updates that make previous versions appear dated [1 mark for a valid example]

practice_questions.text: Give two specific environmental impacts of burning fossil fuels to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per specific mechanism up to 2 (vague phrases score 0):
• Combustion releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming / climate change
• Releases sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain and damages vegetation and aquatic ecosystems
• Releases particulate matter, which causes respiratory health problems in nearby populations
• Extraction (mining, drilling) causes habitat loss and risk of oil spills affecting wildlife

practice_questions.text:
A design engineer is specifying the maintenance requirements for a steel gearbox housing that will be installed outdoors at a coastal wind turbine site.

Describe three maintenance measures the engineer should specify, explaining the engineering reason for each.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (1 mark per measure + 1 mark for a valid engineering reason, max 2 points fully developed):
• Protective surface coating / galvanising or marine-grade paint system — prevents corrosion of steel housing in the salt-spray coastal environment; without coating, rust will penetrate the surface rapidly
• Sealed bearings with defined grease-life replacement interval — maintains lubrication at gear shaft bearings; without regular lubrication, friction and heat increase leading to premature bearing failure
• Defined service interval with oil-level check and gear-oil change — gear oil degrades over time from heat and contamination; regular change prevents abrasive wear of gear teeth
• Wear measurement inspection at each service — allows early detection of gear-tooth wear before it reaches a critical level that would cause sudden failure

practice_questions.text:
Branton Structures Ltd is designing a 30-year maintenance plan for a road bridge. The bridge deck uses reinforced concrete supported on structural steel beams, and is exposed to de-icing salt spray in winter.

Evaluate the importance of designing for maintenance in the material choices and service plan for this bridge, considering at least three engineering maintenance concerns.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Addresses at least three distinct maintenance concerns with specific engineering reasons. For example: (1) Corrosion of steel beams from de-icing salt — must specify stainless steel fasteners, protective paint system, regular inspection and re-painting schedule; neglecting this is the most common cause of bridge structural degradation. (2) Concrete carbonation and chloride ingress — de-icing salt allows chloride ions to penetrate, causing rebar to rust and spall the concrete cover; design must specify minimum cover depth and regular chloride-content testing. (3) Wear of road surface and expansion joints — joints allow thermal expansion but collect grit that causes accelerated wear; service plan must include joint inspection and clearing. Response evaluates the cost of maintaining correctly against the cost of premature replacement or failure, and reaches a justified conclusion about the importance of designing maintenance in from the outset.
Secure (5-6): Three concerns identified with reasonable engineering reasoning; evaluation present.
Developing (3-4): Two concerns covered; reasoning may be partial or generic.
Emerging (1-2): One concern named; no engineering justification.

practice_questions.text:
Helion Power Ltd is comparing two sites for a new energy generation facility: Site A is suitable for a tidal barrage, Site B is suitable for a biomass power station.

Discuss the environmental impact of each option on the local ecosystem and the wider environment. In your answer, use specific engineering and environmental mechanisms rather than general statements.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Discuss Impact on Society and Environment
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Tidal barrage: predictable power output tied to tidal cycle (not 24/7); no operational greenhouse emissions; but the barrage changes water flow and sediment transport in the estuary, potentially destroying intertidal habitats (mudflats, salt marsh) used by migratory birds; affects fish migration routes. Wider environment benefit: displaces fossil-fuel generation and associated CO2. Biomass: burns organic material releasing CO2, but if biomass is sustainably managed (regrown at the same rate as burned) the net CO2 is approximately zero over the growth cycle; transport of biomass adds vehicle emissions; risk of land-use change if non-local biomass is imported (deforestation). Response identifies that neither option has zero impact and evaluates which impact type (local ecosystem vs global climate) is more significant, reaching a reasoned conclusion.
Secure (5-6): Both options covered with at least two specific mechanisms each; some comparison made.
Developing (3-4): Both options described but mechanisms vague; comparison limited.
Emerging (1-2): One option described or both described only in generic terms.

practice_questions.text:
A student sees a component in a circuit diagram. It has three connections, with an arrow on one of them pointing outward.

Identify the component.
practice_questions.marks:
Transistor (NPN transistor) [1 mark]
Note: 'resistor' is a common wrong answer — resistors have two connections and are shown as a box or zigzag.

practice_questions.text:
Complete the truth table for an AND gate:

A | B | Output
0 | 0 | ___
0 | 1 | ___
1 | 0 | ___
1 | 1 | ___
practice_questions.marks:
0 | 0 | 0 [correct]
0 | 1 | 0 [correct]
1 | 0 | 0 [correct]
1 | 1 | 1 [correct]
1 marks awarded for each pair correct:
- Rows 1 and 2 correct [1 mark]
- Row 3 correct [1 mark]
- Row 4 correct [1 mark]
[3 marks total — must use 0 and 1 not yes/no or true/false]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an analogue signal and a digital signal. Give one example of a sensor that produces each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- Analogue signal: varies continuously between two values, can take any value (e.g. thermistor output, LDR output, microphone output).
- Digital signal: has only two states — HIGH (1) or LOW (0) (e.g. push-button switch, reed switch, digital encoder output).
[2 marks — must distinguish 'continuous range' vs 'two states' and give a valid example for each]

practice_questions.text:
A security alarm system uses two sensors: a door sensor (input A) and a motion sensor (input B). The alarm should sound only when both sensors are triggered at the same time.

(a) Name the logic gate that should be used.
(b) Complete the truth table for this system.
(c) Explain why an OR gate would not be suitable.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
(a) AND gate [1 mark]
(b) Truth table:
A=0,B=0 → 0; A=0,B=1 → 0; A=1,B=0 → 0; A=1,B=1 → 1 [1 mark for all rows correct]
(c) An OR gate output is HIGH when either A OR B is triggered alone — the alarm would sound even if only one sensor is triggered, causing false alarms. [2 marks — 1 for identifying OR would activate on a single sensor, 1 for linking to the consequence (false alarms)]
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: State the function of an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) and explain where it is positioned in a programmable electronic system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- An ADC converts a continuous analogue voltage (from a sensor) into a discrete digital binary number.
- It is placed between the analogue sensor and the microcontroller/digital processor, so that the sensor output can be read by the digital system.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Fenwick Electronic Systems Ltd is designing a temperature-monitoring unit for a food refrigeration cabinet. The unit must trigger an alarm if the temperature rises above 5°C. The system uses a thermistor, an ADC, a microcontroller and a buzzer.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using a thermistor as the temperature-sensing element for this application. In your answer, consider at least one alternative sensor.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains that an NTC thermistor’s resistance falls as temperature rises, and that a potential divider produces a temperature-dependent analogue voltage; this must be converted by an ADC before the microcontroller can process it. Evaluates advantages (cheap, small, robust, wide temperature range, fast response). Evaluates disadvantages (non-linear response — resistance doesn't drop proportionally with temperature, requires calibration; analogue output needs ADC). Considers an alternative (digital temperature sensor IC such as DS18B20): direct digital output (no ADC needed), pre-calibrated, higher accuracy. Compares on cost, accuracy, integration complexity and food-safety regulatory context. Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Correct description of thermistor function, at least two advantages and one disadvantage, one alternative with brief comparison. Conclusion present.

Developing (3-4): Basic description of thermistor. One advantage and one disadvantage. Limited alternative.

Emerging (1-2): Simple identification of thermistor with minimal reasoning.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the annealing process?
A) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled rapidly in water
B) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled slowly inside the furnace
C) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled in still air
D) Low-carbon steel is heated in a carbon-rich atmosphere and then quenched
practice_questions.marks: B) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled slowly inside the furnace [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of tempering and explain why it is always carried out after hardening.
practice_questions.marks:
Tempering reduces the brittleness of hardened steel [1 mark].
Hardening produces a fully martensitic structure that is very hard but brittle and would crack under impact; tempering partially converts the martensite to a tougher structure so the component can withstand service loads without shattering [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a steel gear wheel used in a gearbox is case hardened rather than fully hardened throughout its section.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clearly explains both what case hardening achieves (hard surface + tough core) and why full through-hardening is unsuitable (would be too brittle, gear tooth would shatter under bending load), linking both to the specific service requirements of a gear wheel.

Secure (3-4 marks): Both surface hardness (wear resistance) and core toughness identified, with some explanation of the consequence of full hardening. May be underdeveloped on one point.

Developing (1-2 marks): One property mentioned with limited explanation; little link to the gear wheel application.

Content that may be credited:
- Gear teeth experience high contact stresses on their surface from meshing with other gears — the surface must be hard to resist wear and pitting.
- Gear teeth also experience bending loads at the root — the core must be tough to resist these without fracture.
- Full through-hardening would produce a uniform martensite structure throughout — extremely hard but brittle — the tooth would snap under bending rather than deform.
- Case hardening uses a low-carbon steel core (tough, ductile) with a high-carbon case diffused to a depth of typically 0.5–1.5 mm, then quenched to harden only the case.
- Result: surface has the hardness (typically 60–62 HRC) for wear resistance; the core retains toughness to carry the bending load.

practice_questions.text:
A low-carbon steel shaft has been cold-drawn to a reduced diameter. The manufacturing engineer wants to remove the internal stresses and restore ductility before further forming.

Identify the most appropriate heat treatment and describe the process stages.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Most appropriate heat treatment: Annealing [1 mark].
Process stages (award one mark each for any three):
- Heat the steel above its upper critical temperature (e.g. 830–880 °C for low-carbon steel) and soak until uniform temperature throughout
- Turn off the furnace and allow the steel to cool very slowly inside the furnace (do NOT remove and air-cool)
- The slow cooling produces a coarse, ductile grain structure with minimal internal stress
- The resulting steel is soft and ductile, suitable for further cold working
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the cooling rate after heating affects the resulting properties of a carbon steel. Refer to normalising and hardening in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Normalising: heated above critical temperature, cooled in still air (moderate cooling rate). Result: fine, uniform grain structure; moderate hardness and toughness; internal stresses relieved.
Hardening: heated above critical temperature, quenched rapidly in water or oil (very fast cooling rate). Result: martensitic structure; maximum hardness but brittle; high internal stresses.
Comparison: the faster the cooling rate, the harder (and more brittle) the result. Still-air cooling (normalising) gives a balanced microstructure; rapid quenching (hardening) locks in maximum hardness at the cost of ductility.
Consequence: a normalised steel is used for general engineering applications; a hardened-then-tempered steel is used for cutting tools, springs and bearings.
[6 marks — award for developed comparative points. At least two properties compared for each process. No marks for description in isolation.]

practice_questions.text: Kestrel Tool Works Ltd manufactures high-speed steel twist drills that must be hard enough to cut mild steel but must not shatter when loaded. Describe the heat treatment sequence the manufacturer should apply after initial machining.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
